root: ^The French patrol appears suddenly from the woods ahead - twenty mounted men-at-arms, professional soldiers in good armor. They spot you at the same moment.
^"English dogs!" their leader shouts. "You've come to the wrong land to die!"
^Sir Robert immediately forms a battle line. "Archers! Loose arrows! Men-at-arms, prepare to charge!"
^"Good!" Sir Robert agrees. "Take twenty men and hit their flank. Archers will keep them busy."
^The English longbowmen respond instantly, arrows darkening the sky around the French commander.
^"Smart," Sir Robert nods. "Let them waste their charge on our defenses."
^You lead the charge, your horse thundering across the field. The French patrol turns to meet you, but they're surprised by your aggressiveness.
^Lances shatter and swords flash as the two forces collide. You're in the thick of it, your sword finding gaps in French armor.
^Your men follow your lead, driving deeper into the French formation. The patrol starts to break.
^"No!" you shout. "We have them! Keep fighting!"
^You spot the French commander trying to rally his men. "Take him alive!"
^The English arrows find their mark. The French commander falls from his horse, multiple arrows in his chest. The patrol hesitates, leaderless.
^Your men roar approval and surge forward. The remaining French soldiers try to flee but are cut down.
^Some French soldiers throw down their weapons. "Mercy! We surrender!"
^"Let them go," Sir Robert decides. "We have wounded to tend to and loot to gather."
^The road narrows between thick woods - perfect ambush territory. Too late, you realize the danger as arrows fly from both sides.
^French infantry emerge from the woods - fifty men, professional soldiers. They've planned this carefully.
^"Madness," Sir Robert counters. "We don't know how many are in there. Hold formation!"
^The English longbowmen respond, arrows flying back into the woods. Screams indicate they're finding targets.
^"Good thinking," Sir Robert agrees. "We need better ground. Back to the hill!"
^The forest becomes a deadly exchange of arrows. English longbows outrange the French crossbows, giving you an advantage.
^French soldiers fall as English arrows find their marks. The ambush is turning against them.
^Sir Robert leads the charge. The French infantry, caught in the open between volleys, are vulnerable.
^The English archers maintain their deadly rhythm. The French start to break.
^"Too risky," Sir Robert decides. "Let the arrows do their work. We're winning this exchange."
^A French scout party appears on the ridge ahead - ten light cavalry, outriders for a larger force. They've spotted you.
^"English!" their leader shouts. "The main army will be here soon!"
^"Agreed," Sir Robert nods. "We can't let them warn anyone. Fast pursuit!"
^"Dangerous," Sir Robert cautions. "They know where we are now. We'll have French troops on us in hours."
^"Good idea," Sir Robert agrees. "They might know French dispositions."
^The French scouts flee, but your lighter cavalry is faster. The chase is on across the rolling countryside.
^You gain on the rearmost scout, your horse eating up the distance. He looks back in terror.
^The scout pulls up his horse, surrendering. His companions continue to flee.
^Your lance strikes true, and the scout falls. His companions see this and ride harder.
^You push your horse harder, targeting the French commander. If he falls, the others will panic.
^The village you're raiding fights back - not with soldiers, but with desperate peasants led by the local lord. Fifty men, poorly armed but determined.
^"For Normandy!" the lord shouts. "Drive out the English!"
^Sir Robert laughs. "Peasants against professional soldiers? This will be short."
^"Good thinking," Sir Robert agrees. "Without their lord, they'll break."
^The English longbowmen draw and loose. The peasant charge falters under the arrow storm.
^The peasants charge with desperate courage - pitchforks, axes, and hunting bows against professional men-at-arms.
^The result is never in doubt. English discipline and armor prove decisive. The peasants break after minimal casualties.
^"No," Sir Robert decides. "The dead can't pay tribute. Round up the survivors."
^The local lord tries to flee but is captured by your men. A valuable hostage.
^"Definitely," Sir Robert agrees. "They resisted - they need to learn the price of defiance."
^The castle you've been raiding finally sallies forth - fifty professional soldiers led by an experienced knight. They're trying to break your siege of their outskirts.
^"Enough of your raiding!" the castle commander shouts. "Face real soldiers!"
^Sir Robert forms a battle line. "Steady, men! Let them come to us!"
^The English longbowmen loose volley after volley. The castle soldiers advance under a hail of arrows.
^"Good idea," Sir Robert agrees. "Send cavalry around their sides. Pin them with infantry."
^The two forces crash together in a clash of steel and determination. Professional soldiers on both sides, this will be a real fight.
^You're in the center of the fighting, your sword busy parrying and striking. The castle soldiers are tough, well-trained, and well-equipped.
^You lead the push, driving deeper into their formation. The castle line starts to bend.
^"Never!" Sir Robert shouts. "We have them! Keep fighting!"
^The castle standard bearer goes down under your sword. The castle soldiers hesitate.
^You're trying to cross a river when French forces appear on the opposite bank - archers and men-at-arms, determined to prevent your crossing.
^"No English dogs cross this river!" their commander shouts. "Turn back or die!"
^"Madness," Sir Robert says. "We'd be sitting ducks in the water."
^The English longbowmen respond, arrows forcing the French to take cover.
^"Good thinking," Sir Robert agrees. "No point fighting on unfavorable ground."
^English arrows keep the French pinned while your engineers quickly construct a makeshift bridge.
^The French, unable to effectively respond, watch helplessly as your forces prepare to cross.
^"Agreed," Sir Robert nods. "Once we have a foothold, the rest can cross safely."
^"Too risky," Sir Robert cautions. "If the bridge fails, we lose everyone."
^"Definitely," Sir Robert agrees. "No point letting them follow us."
^The French attack your camp at night - a desperate attempt to catch you unprepared. Torches light the chaos as soldiers pour into your encampment.
^"English! Wake up! We're under attack!" Sir Robert's voice cuts through the confusion.
^Your men quickly organize, forming a shield wall around the supply wagons.
^"Too risky in the dark," Sir Robert cautions. "We don't know how many there are."
^Good idea - the additional light reveals the French force size. About a hundred men.
^Your men hold a defensive perimeter, shields locked together. The French attack repeatedly but can't break the shield wall.
^The fighting is desperate in the torchlight. English discipline holds against French ferocity.
^"Now!" Sir Robert commands. The shield wall opens and your men charge out.
^The French attacks become weaker as casualties mount. Their morale is failing.
^The English archers, positioned on the wagons, shoot over the shield wall into the French rear.
^You're covering the main force's withdrawal when French cavalry appears - fast, professional soldiers trying to catch your stragglers.
^"Form rearguard!" Sir Robert commands. "Buy the main force time to escape!"
^Your men form a battle line across the road. The French cavalry approaches at a gallop.
^"Good tactic," Sir Robert agrees. "Disengage before they can bring full force to bear."
^"Excellent idea," Sir Robert nods. "The woods on our right - we can hit their flank."
^Your fighting withdrawal works perfectly. You engage just long enough to delay the French, then fall back before they can bring overwhelming force to bear.
^The French commander grows increasingly frustrated as your force slips away, always just out of reach.
^"No," Sir Robert decides. "Our job is to delay, not to die. Keep falling back."
^"Not yet," Sir Robert cautions. "Wait for the right moment."
^"Agreed," Sir Robert nods. "The main force should be safe by now. Let's go."
^The skirmishes are over for now, but they've taken their toll. Your force is battered but victorious, richer in plunder and experience but poorer in men and morale.

^Each fight has increased the heat - the French now know you're a serious threat, not just raiders but a professional fighting force. They'll respond with stronger forces, better coordination, and greater determination.
^The chevauchee continues, but the easy targets are gone. From here on, every encounter will be more dangerous, every French response more determined.
